memory_update.text: For AI, preserve a broad chain view: demand and capex, accelerators, HBM, advanced packaging, substrates, ABF/T-glass, MLCCs and dielectric powders, optics, power delivery, cooling, data-center electrical infrastructure, permitting, and disclosure quality.

Highest-priority bottleneck nodes are advanced substrates, ABF/T-glass inputs, HBM plus advanced packaging/test/inspection, AI-server high-end MLCCs, MLCC dielectric powders, optical interconnect components, and data-center electrical infrastructure.

Do not let GPU, hyperscaler, or software leaders dominate the map. Use them as demand validators, then follow pull-through into underfollowed materials, equipment, qualification, and regulated infrastructure nodes.

Track capex revisions, customer prepayments, qualification wins, lead-time extensions, price increases, capacity expansions, and earnings comments that mention AI-server, HBM, advanced packaging, optics, or data-center power.

Regulatory or policy catalysts include export controls, grid and data-center permitting, utility interconnection reform, and potential disclosure changes around commercially entangled AI cloud revenue.

Need primary-source verification for substrate supplier customer advance payments, ABF allocation priority, T-glass supplier identity/share, MLCC per-server content, and dielectric-powder market share. Current evidence includes third-party articles and cached Serenity context.
For optics and signal-integrity nodes, verify AI datacenter revenue mix, customer concentration, backlog duration, pricing, and whether growth offsets telecom or industrial cyclicality.

For power, cooling, and regulated infrastructure nodes, later layers should collect utility filings, interconnection queue data, transformer and switchgear lead times, data-center permitting records, and backlog commentary from electrical equipment suppliers.

FORM maps to the AI/HBM known-good-die test node; relationship is plausible but currently needs primary-source confirmation of HBM probe-card revenue durability, customer concentration, and margin impact.
CAMT maps to advanced-packaging inspection/metrology; next layer should verify explicit HBM, chiplet, OSAT, and CoWoS-like exposure in company disclosures.
ONTO maps to process control and metrology for HBM4 and advanced packaging; needs evidence that HBM4 selection or advanced-packaging tools convert into multi-quarter volume orders.
AIXA.DE maps to compound-semiconductor epitaxy tools upstream of lasers for AI optical interconnects; this is an indirect but potentially underfollowed AI infrastructure relationship.
VECO maps to diversified advanced-packaging and compound-semiconductor process equipment; AI exposure should remain hypothesis-level until revenue materiality is verified.
KLIC maps to advanced-packaging bonding tools, but legacy wire-bond cyclicality may dominate; promote only if thermocompression or other advanced-packaging orders become material.
6981.T maps to AI-server high-end MLCCs/passives with the strongest provided external evidence in this chunk; primary-source verification should focus on AI-server mix, lead times, and pricing power.

AMKR is a reference OSAT advanced-packaging capacity anchor rather than an underfollowed pure-play; useful for public-market mapping of AI/HPC packaging capacity but needs customer and end-market mix verification.
LITE maps to AI datacenter lasers and optical components; evidence must separate 800G/1.6T datacom growth from telecom inventory and pricing cycles.
COHR maps to optical materials, lasers, and transceivers for AI networking; the relationship is diluted by telecom, industrial, debt, and margin factors that require primary-source checks.

The provided external evidence is strongest for Murata and the broader MLCC/passives thesis; most inspection, metrology, probe-card, bonding, OSAT, optical, and compound-semiconductor equipment names require company-level filings, transcripts, and order/backlog checks before Layer 3 promotion.

SMTC should remain in the underfollowed AI optical-networking lane as a hypothesis-level signal-integrity and mixed-signal supplier; promote only if direct datacenter optical, 800G/1.6T, or AI customer revenue evidence appears.

TSEM should remain in the underfollowed silicon-photonics foundry lane; the key gating evidence is whether silicon-photonics programs are meaningfully tied to AI datacenter optical interconnect demand rather than general specialty foundry mix.

ETN and VRT are reference leaders for AI power/cooling infrastructure and should be used as valuation and demand benchmarks for smaller electrical, thermal, and construction candidates rather than treated as underfollowed discoveries.

PWR maps to the grid-interconnection and utility-construction bottleneck. AI exposure is second-order and must be separated from broader electrification, utility hardening, renewables, and transmission capex.

FIX maps to specialized data-center mechanical/electrical contracting and cooling-installation capacity. The stock remains hypothesis-level until datacenter backlog share, project margins, and labor constraints are verified.

NVDA, AVGO, TSM, ASML, and ANET should be retained only as demand, architecture, capex, and pull-through reference anchors for bottleneck discovery in HBM, advanced packaging, optics, passives, power, cooling, and grid infrastructure.

Direct primary-source evidence is missing for SMTC AI optical revenue, TSEM silicon-photonics AI customer programs, PWR datacenter-specific grid backlog, and FIX datacenter backlog share. These gaps should be addressed before Layer 3 scoring.

Market-pricing checks are still incomplete for this chunk: market cap, revenue multiple, EBITDA multiple, analyst coverage, short interest, AI-related share-price move, and relative valuation versus reference leaders need to be added.
MSFT should remain in the AI funnel only as a hyperscaler demand and revenue-quality reference; do not rank it as an underfollowed Serenity bottleneck candidate.

GOOGL should remain a capex, TPU/custom ASIC, cloud demand, and supplier pull-through reference; the relevant Serenity alpha search should occur in substrate, packaging, HBM, optics, power, and cooling suppliers.
AMZN should remain an AWS AI infrastructure and custom silicon demand anchor; verify Trainium/Inferentia supplier pull-through rather than treating AMZN as the chokepoint.
PLTR is a high-attention software reference for AI workflow revenue-quality checks; require production deployment and durable expansion evidence before promoting software peers.

SNOW is a high-attention data-platform reference for AI consumption durability; use it to benchmark niche data workflow candidates but require evidence that AI workloads are increasing net retention and consumption.

Layer 2B for this chunk lacks primary-source verification from the latest company filings and earnings transcripts for MSFT, GOOGL, AMZN, PLTR, and SNOW; current mapping relies on cached Layer 1 relationships plus general SEC petition evidence on cloud revenue disclosure risk.
Market-pricing checks remain missing for all five tickers: current market cap, forward revenue or earnings multiple, analyst coverage, recent AI-related price move, and embedded expectation risk.

For the underfollowed lane, this reference chunk should be connected downstream to smaller suppliers in MLCCs, dielectric powders, advanced substrates, ABF/T-glass, optical components, power equipment, liquid cooling, data-center construction, and niche AI data workflow software.

summary: Split Layer 2 synthesis. Industry-chain map and catalyst layer for the AI theme. The map intentionally does not start with high-attention GPU, hyperscaler, or mega-cap software leaders. It decomposes AI into demand, compute, memory, advanced packaging, substrates, optical networking, power delivery, passive components, materials, equipment, certification gates, data-center infrastructure, and disclosure/regulatory nodes. The highest bottleneck scores are assigned to layers with concentrated suppliers, long qualification cycles, hard-to-expand process know-how, scarce materials, or yield-sensitive capacity: advanced substrates and ABF/T-glass inputs, HBM plus advanced packaging/test/inspection, AI-server high-end MLCCs and upstream dielectric powders, optical interconnect components/equipment, and power/cooling infrastructure.

supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Training and inference workloads drive the entire chain: accelerator purchases, HBM demand, networking bandwidth, storage, power, cooling, and cloud revenue. This node is high-attention, so it should be used as demand validation rather than as the main bottleneck hunt.

supply_chain_map.node: Hyperscaler and sovereign AI capex budgets
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Cloud providers, large internet platforms, enterprises, and governments translate AI demand into purchase orders for servers, networking, data centers, and power. Budget changes can rapidly affect the whole chain.

GPUs and custom AI ASICs are the visible compute layer. They determine pull-through into HBM, substrates, CoWoS-like packaging, power delivery, optics, and cooling. However, this node is crowded and high-attention.

High-bandwidth memory is necessary for large-model training and high-performance inference. HBM growth increases demand for advanced DRAM processes, stacking, testing, substrates, and packaging capacity.

AI accelerators increasingly require 2.5D/3D integration, interposers, HBM-to-logic assembly, high-yield bonding, and complex package substrates. Capacity additions are expensive, yield-sensitive, and customer-qualified.

As AI packages become larger, denser, and more expensive, yield control becomes more valuable. Inspection and metrology suppliers can sit one layer below the obvious HBM/foundry story and may benefit from rising process complexity.

Defective dies inside expensive multi-die AI packages can destroy package economics. More HBM stacks and chiplets increase test intensity and make qualified probe/test consumables a potential bottleneck.

AI accelerators need larger, higher-layer-count, finer-feature substrates. Supplier qualification can take years, yields are hard to master, and customer co-funding or advance payments can indicate scarce capacity.

ABF film is a critical material for high-end substrates. If substrate makers depend on a limited ABF supply base, material allocation can become a hidden constraint below the visible AI accelerator layer.

supply_chain_map.node: T-glass and ultra-low-CTE glass cloth for substrates
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: High-end substrate glass cloth can be concentrated and process-knowledge-driven. If one supplier dominates advanced T-glass, it may represent a low-attention materials bottleneck under AI accelerators.

AI servers and racks require many more high-performance capacitors to stabilize high-current, fast-transient power delivery. The bottleneck is not commodity MLCCs but small, high-capacitance, low-ESR, low-ESL parts that few suppliers can mass-produce.

supply_chain_map.node: MLCC dielectric powders and barium titanate
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Upstream ceramic powders determine the performance envelope of high-end MLCCs. If AI-server MLCC demand tightens, suppliers of nano-scale barium titanate and dielectric materials may capture bottleneck economics before the market fully sees them.

supply_chain_map.node: Voltage regulators, power stages, and board-level power delivery
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI accelerators draw large and fast-changing currents. Rack and board power architecture drives demand for VRMs, power modules, connectors, busbars, passives, and thermal design.

Higher rack density and higher accelerator power require cold plates, CDUs, pumps, manifolds, heat exchangers, and facility-level thermal integration. Qualification and reliability matter because downtime risk is high.

Large AI clusters require low-latency, high-bandwidth east-west traffic. 800G, 1.6T, co-packaged optics, and related optical modules create demand for lasers, photonics, DSPs, transceiver assembly, and testing.
Optical module ramps depend on qualified lasers, modulators, drivers, photodiodes, and materials. This node can be hidden inside broader telecom, industrial photonics, or component companies.

Optical and photonic components require compound semiconductor epitaxy capacity. Epitaxy equipment suppliers sit upstream from optical module leaders and may be lower-attention beneficiaries of AI networking.

Even when optical designs exist, scale production requires qualified manufacturing, assembly, testing, yield control, and customer-specific processes. Contract manufacturers and specialized suppliers can be hidden bottlenecks.

supply_chain_map.node: Networking switches, NICs, retimers, DSPs, and signal integrity components
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI clusters need high-speed switching and signal integrity around optical links. The bottleneck can appear in analog/mixed-signal components rather than headline switch silicon.

Rack-scale systems such as GPU clusters require mechanical, electrical, power, cooling, firmware, and logistics integration. Margins may be thinner than component bottlenecks, but ramps can reveal stress in supply.
Grid interconnection, transformers, switchgear, UPS systems, generators, power distribution units, and substation equipment can constrain AI data-center deployment even when chips are available.

supply_chain_map.node: Utility power, interconnection queues, and regulated energy assets
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI data-center growth increasingly depends on available power, permitting, grid upgrades, and utility/regulator approvals. This node may hide value in regulated assets and infrastructure suppliers rather than semiconductor names.

supply_chain_map.node: Data-center real estate, permitting, and water access
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Land, power, water, zoning, environmental review, and local opposition can delay AI data-center capacity. These constraints affect deployment timing and cloud revenue recognition.

supply_chain_map.node: Cloud revenue disclosure and commercial entanglement
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI infrastructure revenue quality may depend on whether cloud revenue comes from independent customers or customers financially supported by the cloud provider or related AI ecosystem participants. Disclosure changes could affect perceived demand quality.

supply_chain_map.node: Distribution, channel allocation, and customer certification gates
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: For materials, components, and tools, access to qualified customers, allocation priority, and long certification cycles can matter as much as technical capability. These gates are often under-disclosed and underfollowed.
